subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Although the leader of the opposition has a fine legal experience, he has not the military background of General Crerar. I would rather suggest to the minister that he appoint the leader of the opposition as judge-advocate-general if there is a vacancy in that office at any time.
Having the information from the leader of the opposition that it was on his recommendation that the training period was extended from one month to four, who was the military genius who advised the Minister of National Defence himself to decide, in virtue of the powers granted to him by an order in council of very wide scope, to extend that period of training from four months to an indefinite time? I do not know if it was done according to the rules of astrology, or table-turning, or inspiration, or by the ouija board, but it was done. What surprises me is the complete indifference of the Canadian people in that regard. There is a rule that is known to everyone; it is that a delegate cannot delegate, delegatus non potest delegare. The country has conferred power on the government by legislation, and the government takes advantage of this delegation of power to pass orders in council. But how is it that the government can go so far as to transfer to a single individual powers that were granted to them by parliament, even if that individual is the Minister of National Defence? And the more so because the minister was entitled to decide by a stroke of the pen matters that had previously been decided only by orders in council. It seems strange. But of course the Canadian people do not now have the same interest in constitutional matters that they had at the time of Mercier in Quebec, Mowat in Ontario, and other leaders of earlier days. Then they had information that was much more complete than that of to-day, and they held to the British doctrine and the great British parliamentary tradition.
What is the law? The law is just a sheet of paper. We have no more bound statutes. It takes a long time to secure orders in council of a legislative nature. I think it was my friend the hon. member for Lake Centre who asked for the production of all orders in council of a legislative nature, not of an administrative nature, and he was told that that distinction had not been made and that it would take a tremendous time to secure those orders in council duly classified. Well, sir, I have these rules that have been published in book form, small volumes that are really the law of the land in this country, because the legislation that we are enacting now is only for monetary matters; all the legislation we have which binds Canadian

citizens just the same as Gulliver was tied at Lilliput by the dwarfs, is by order in council. The result is to create among the people of Canada disrespect for legislation, as well as to create embarrassment for all those who have to explain the law to either their clients or their constituents. So I regret very much that such wide powers over individuals who do not come within the jurisdiction of the hon. gentleman should have been given to the Minister of National Defence, because his department proper has no authority over the recruits until they are called to the colours and are actually in the army. Those powers, should have been given to the Minister of National War Services, if the government, had been empowered by us to transfer such powers to a single minister.
If we do not have order now, what will we have in the aftermath, when the war is over? It is a most incredible situation. Either there is order in the Department of National Defence, or there is not. If there is order, it should be very simple for the minister to give the information requested as to the functions and cost of each of these branches. That is a reasonable thing; there is no libel or slander in that. It is the most ordinary thing in the world; and if there is no such order, then a change is necessary. We cannot get away from that. If the minister sees clearly what is going on in his department; if he has a chart showing the various occupations of those under him here in Ottawa, let him supply that chart to all hon. members so that there may be no embarrassment whatever when they have to deal with anyone in the Department of National Defence. This seems very clear and very easy, but we have not obtained that information from the minister. I am quite willing to sit down and listen to the hon. gentleman if he has no objection to placing such a chart upon Hansard, because that will be very informative.
What is the trouble with the Department of National Defence in Ottawa? It suffers from elephantiasis. I need not describe that illness, but when one is afflicted with it some parts of the body grow too large, especially the feet. The feet become bigger than the head, and it is incurable. Of course it is a disease that occurs usually in tropical countries, but since everything under the sun is changed here it is not surprising that it should occur in Canada. We are told at times when we discuss these matters of dollars and cents that we are not patriotic.
I should like those who hold this view to repeat that contention before their constituents when those constituents are called upon to pay taxes. Hon. gentlemen will have

War Appropriation
to have very sweet tongues to have that suggestion accepted by the Canadian people. I have also been told from high quarters that I have shown disrespect to those who have exposed their lives in an actual theatre of war, when I have complained about some people on the general staff. But even if I were cruel to the branch of the judge-advocate-general, I would not do harm to many who had thus exposed their lives in a theatre of war, because such are scarce in that branch, though the branch is large. There is less reason for the existence of that branch now than at any time previously, for obvious reasons. Previously the main duty of this branch was to draft and examine contracts for purchases made by the Department of National Defence. That was in the old days, before the minister had suffered capitis deminutio, a reduction of the head. Like my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, sometimes I feel compelled to use a dead tongue in order to find the proper legal phrase.
During the last war, and until a comparatively short time ago, the Minister of National Defence was responsible for all purchases made by his department. Then the judge-advocate-general's branch was much more important than it is now, and in it were some jurists of considerable legal ability, who were able to draft contracts and give the minister sound legal opinions. Now, however, there are no more contracts of this kind. When a purchase is made it is done by filling out requisition forms, so the Minister of National Defence has no more to do in that regard than any deputy minister or other official who makes out a requisition for what he needs. The purchases are not made by the Department of National Defence. That department must send a requisition to the Department of Munitions and Supply, which obtains whatever is required. Then the bill is paid not by the Department of Munitions and Supply, but by the Department of Finance. Have you ever seen anything like that, Mr. Chairman, in your wide experience as a parliamentarian? Of course this is the way things go, and people are indifferent to it. They say, "Let it go. It is all right. This is war time." Of course it is war time, but we want the government to be as strong in war time as it should be in peace time, and we want order in all departments.
I find that some people are very touchy. It is impossible to say a word of criticism about anyone without having someone say that you not only show bad manners but are also a coward to attack someone who is
not present, as though the minister did not represent all those under him. There is no personal grudge against anyone, but we want all those in the Department of National Defence as well as those in other departments to have respect for parliament. It is my idea to preach respect for parliament and parliamentary institutions to all those in the civil service and all high officials who are in the dominion's pay.
What is our business? It is our business here as members of the House of Commons to act as intermediaries between the government and the taxpayers, so that there may be no abuse. When there is a general meeting of the shareholders of a company, any shareholder is entitled to ask the management for information about any expenditure. We are not hard on the minister; we take good care of him, and we want him to have the least possible difficulty in administering his department. I make these observations in accordance with that reference in the Bible where it is stated that the wounds of those who like are better than the kisses of those who hate.
W'hen I say this I am not referring to the leader of the opposition. I only repeat those words of wisdom which have the sanction of time immemorial. I wonder whether the minister is in a good enough mood to give us a charter of the Department of National Defence, and whether he will explain to us the functions of all branches in his department. This is most essential, because over a year ago I asked him to supply hon. members of parliament with the King's Regulations and Orders, as amended. All hon. members know, of course, that those regulations are printed in the Canada Gazette, but because of the work we have to do, it is quite troublesome for us to cut the issues of the Gazette, and make a scrapbook. That is done in the department, and I therefore ask the minister if possible to supply all hon. members with a copy of the amended regulations. I have asked the same question three times. Finally the minister told me that in spite of the order in council passed years ago, one which is respected by all departments except the Department of National Defence, and is to the effect that upon request any member of parliament may secure not only one but two copies, one in English and one in French, of any matter circulated by the king's printer, it was not the practice of his department to do that. We are not supplied with those important regulations by the Department of National Defence. When the house sits in committee we ask for information, and it is not given to us.

But, so far as I am
concerned the hon. member has asked for two things. First, he has asked for the King's Regulations and Orders, and he has also asked for a statement with regard to the expenditures of each department. He has taken twenty-five minutes to ask for those two things.
I want to say first that the accounts are not made up so that one may have all the expenditures of the adjutant-general's branch under one heading. The adjutant-general has to do with promotions, pay, medical services and auxiliary services. Those are some of the most important things with which he has to deal. You would have to take not only the pay of the officers in all the branches, but all the money paid out by those branches, in order to bring the whole expenditures of the department within the terms of those four heads of branches. The same applies to the chief of the general staff.
The chief of the general staff has to do particularly with training and operations. Under him is the intelligence branch, the operational branch and training, in a very large way. He has the job of coordinating the other three chief branches, namely the adjutant-general, the master-general of the ordnance, and the quartermaster-general.
The quartermaster-general has to do with the provision of accommodation for our forces, the provision of engineering services, the provision of transportation, and the provision of food. The master-general of the ordnance has to do with the provision of equipment of all sorts, whether it be for actual fighting operations, for ordnance, munitions or anything of that kind. The accounts are not kept so that you can take any of those branches and find out how much the master-general of the ordnance spent. You would want to find out how much is paid for pay and allowances, clothing, munitions, and things of that kind. The fact that it happened to be paid out under the branch of the master-general of the ordnance means nothing at all, and would give no information of any use whatever.
I say to my hon. friend with regard to the King's Regulations and Orders that the

French edition was printed, as I understand it, on April 10, and I shall be glad to see that a free copy is sent to the hon. member, and a copy of the English regulations as well.
